The appellant filed a suit being Title Suit No. 157 of 1965 in the 6th Court of Munsif, Dacca against Azharuddin Ahmed, the predecessor-in-interest of the respondents for ejectment stating, inter alia, that the holding No. 43 Panch Bhai Ghat Lane within Police Station Sutrapur, Dacca originally belonged to one Upendra Kumar. Roy and his co-sharers from whom the appellant acquired 16 annas interest on the basis of two documents namely, a deed of lease dated 8.8.1956 and a deed of sale of rent receiving interest dated 9.8.1956 constituting sale of the property within the knowledge of the monthly tenant Azharuddin Ahmed but since then the latter instead of paying rent directly to the appellant started depositing the same with the House Rent Controller although the appellant was willing and ready to accept the rent direct from him. The tenant Azharuddin was depositing rent with a motive to create confusion as to the title of the appellant and thereby to grab the property himself. The deposit of rent with the House Rent Controller was not a legal and valid discharge of liability in respect of payment of rent. He thus was a defaulter. Moreover, the appellant's another ground was that no bonafide required the premises for his family accommodation after necessary reconstruction of the same. The tenant, was, therefore, asked to vacate the premises. On refusal of the tenant to comply with the request of the appellant, the latter served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act through his lawyer and determined the tenancy. 

 6. Mr. A. Malek, the learned counsel for the appellant argued that Azharuddin admitted the title of the appellant to the suit premises in an affidavit exhibit D sworn by him in Writ Petition No. 524 of 1964 under Article 98 of the last Constitution which was filed by him for cancellation of an order made by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Dacca directing him to vacate the suit premises. It is to be noted here that the impugned order against which the Writ Petition was filed was passed on the ground that the property in question was forfeited to the Government under Section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The Government treated the transaction between the appellant and his vendors to be a pure and simple lease which was said to have been hit by the provision of section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The High Court in the Writ case found on the basis of the documents, namely, the deed of lease dated 8.8.1956 and the deed of sale of rent receiving interest dated 9. 8. 1956 filed in the Writ Petition that the appellant purchased the suit premises. The documents on the basis of which title was claimed were found to be genuine documents constituting a sale relating to the suit premises and as such the impugned order of forfeiture of: property under section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was declared to have been passed without any legal authority and was of no legal effect and Section 75A was found to be inapplicable. Mr. Malek in that view of the matter strenuously argued that after having admitted the title and interest of the appellant in the suit premises the tenant had no business to deposit the rent with the Rent Controller. Moreover, it has been pointed out by the learned Counsel from the evidence of the tenant that he had deposited the rent without tendering the rent personally or remitting the same by money order with a view to justifying his action in the matter of depositing rent with the Rent Controller. He did not also deposit the transmission cost while he deposited the rent with the Rent Controller. In these circumstances the learned counsel urged that the appellant was not required under the law to bring to the notice of the Rent Controller that the respondent tenant in an affidavit filed by him in a Writ Case admitted appellant's title to the holding with a view to preventing the respondent tenant from depositing the rent. It is in evidence on record that the plaintiff-appellant asked the respondent-tenant to pay rent to him. Hence there was no failure on the part Of the plaintiff appellant to take step to realise rent from the tenant-respondent. In this connection reference has been made to section 19(1), (2) and (3) of the East Pakistan Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 which provides for deposit of rent by the tenant in certain circumstances.
